svg.title: Urna Aberta: one ballot's path from an offline machine to a blockchain and public checking
svg.desc: Animation in 7 scenes of 8 seconds following one ballot. 1: You choose and the machine, offline with no Internet during voting, encrypts the choice. 2: Before the decision, the machine hands over a signed receipt, R7, which shows no candidate. Confirm keeps the ballot encrypted for the tally; test opens the ballot to check the choice, voids that ballot and the voter votes again. R7 is only a symbolic locator code; the full signed receipt and the proofs decide. 3: When polls close, the machine sends one signed batch of encrypted ballots to a contract on a local blockchain (Anvil). The contract checks the signature, the registered machine, one batch per machine and the deadline; it does not verify the cryptographic proofs. 4: Published ballots are added while still encrypted, without opening individual choices. 5: Three of five trustees, who hold parts of the key, publish contributions with proofs to decrypt only the sum. That is the rule of this flow, not a mathematical guarantee: three colluding trustees could decrypt individual ballots. 6: An independent verifier uses the public data, the proofs and your signed receipt to check the ballot's inclusion and recompute the total. Only receipts that are supplied can be checked. 7: Beyond reading the result, you can check inclusion and recompute it. Educational prototype, no claim of absolute secrecy; local blockchain (Anvil).

g.text: To publish the records without exposing each person’s choice.
Why does the receipt come first?
So the machine commits before knowing whether you will test it.
So anyone can check the records and the rules for publishing them.
Why add the votes without opening them?
The tally needs a total, not a list of how each person voted.
So no single trustee has the power to decrypt the total alone.
Why check outside the voting machine?
So you need not just accept the announced total: you can recount it.
You can check the result, not just read it.
Keep your receipt: it lets you check that your ballot was included.
